utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you call the case please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I wish to bid good afternoon to the accused, the counsel of the Defence and the Prosecution, and everyone assisting us, and I will not forget to bid good afternoon to the witness. Regarding the schedule for this hearing, there is one hour 25 minutes left for Madam West. The Chamber is of the opinion, therefore, that Madam West should finish her examination and then we can go until 5 to 4, after which we will have a single pause of 20 minutes, and then we will resume for re-examination. I should also like to ask Defence counsel to make objections only that may be linked to errors in the transcript, or to really important questions. Apart from that, please allow Madam Prosecutor to do her job, in view of the fact that when there was an examination-in-chief there were hardly any objections on the part of the Prosecution. I'll give the floor to the Registrar, which I forgot there are a number of IC numbers to be given.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 4D and 6D has tendered their objections to the list of documents tender by the Prosecution through witness Slobodan Bozic. This list shall be given Exhibit IC 918 and 919 respectively. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Madam West you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, and everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Cross-examination by Ms. West [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. Buljan. Yesterday when we stopped, we were talking about the extent of your knowledge about the events in Mostar in 1993 at a time when you were still living in Posavina. And you had indicated in the course of your testimony that the relationship between the Muslims Croats in Herceg-Bosna versus the relation in Posavina was different. For the record that's page 36810. You had also said there was a incident occurred in mid-1993, and I quote, "so it's of that time that certain situations were somewhat different in comparison to the situation in Posavina." On 36811, I had ask you whether you knew in the latter half of 1993 that the Croats and the Muslims were fighting each other and in response you said, "I heard that there were such problems down there" and then later on in the page you said: "In Mostar, at the time of the incident, there was a certain amount of tension." So in a certain sense there would be a reason for the difference between the situation in Posavina and in Mostar. Sir, do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Twice in the testimony that I just summarised and read out verbatim, you mentioned an incident, you said it twice. Would you agree that the incident that you described in speaking about Mostar is the event of May 9th, the mass arrest and detention of a number of Muslims in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have that particular incident in mind. I meant that generally there was a cooling of relations during that period of time. When I said that there were problems, I didn't have that particular date in mind or that incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember yesterday Judge Antonetti asked you a question, he said: "Given the events in May in Mostar, did these events have any repercussions with regard to the HVO units involved in combat?" And your answer was, "No." In regard to Judge Antonetti's question, the events in May, what did you have in mind when you spoke about that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those activities that were happening down there, the tension, the heightened tensions, had a minimum, I would say, effect, but they did leave some traces in Bosanska Posavina. There were no conflicts. There were no bad words, no problems, but it was discussed a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So is it your testimony that what was going on in Mostar had no effect as to what was going on in the Posavina?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was happening in Mostar did not have a significant effect on what was happening in Posavina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you'll agree with me that when the Muslims and the Croats were fighting each other in Mostar in 1993, the Muslims and the Croats were cooperating with each other in Posavina?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in regard to the question that Judge Antonetti asked you, he said, "did the events in Mostar in May have any repercussions with regard to the HVO units involved in combat" and your answer was, "No." Bearing that question in mind, I want to ask you a slightly different question but it's the same subject matter. Did the events in May have any effect on the number of Muslim soldiers who continued to fight for the HVO in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that there was any significant effect. All that was happening that they heard and saw and that they were told about, I don't think had any significant influence on them, on their remaining there, their combat activities, or their activities in the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you look at 4D 01632. It's in the smaller binder that's directly in front of you. Starts with 4D. Sir, do you have that? This is a list of Muslim -- thank you. This is a list of Muslim soldiers who were in the 2nd HVO Brigade in Mostar who left on May 9th, 1993, and then also some of the subsequent months. This first -- the first listing is about 117 Muslim soldiers who left on that date, and then it's followed up by what appears to be maybe a dozen soldiers who left in the following month. Now, although you've testified that you don't think there was any significant, you've said significant influence on them, that the events had no significant influence on them, to what do you attribute this exodus, this exodus of 117 Muslim soldiers on May 9th in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that those events, or rather heightened tensions in Mostar and the surroundings, did not influence the combat readiness of units in the theatre of war at Orasje. They didn't. Not to a significant extent. Maybe negligibly, but that's not important. This unit is not from that area, the one we are looking at now. It's directly linked to the region we are talking about. I just simply see this list. Now, what motivated them to withdraw from the HVO, is something I can't say. I don't know why they did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, yesterday you testified that you had heard about the ABiH attack on the northern barracks on June 30th. Did that attack or did that event have any effect on the number of Muslims who continued to fight for the HVO and who might ultimately receive welfare benefits from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You mentioned yesterday that you had heard of the June 30th attack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that attack have any effect on the number of Muslim soldiers who continued to fight for the HVO in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you with any certainty and to what extent. There probably was some withdrawal from the brigades after that event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with me if there were some withdrawals as a result of that event, then there would also be an affect on the number of Muslim HVO soldiers who would ultimately claim benefits from the HVO or claim welfare from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All members of the HVO, if they had proof that they were members, and if they had the necessary documents, there was no reason why they wouldn't get all the benefits and the remuneration that was due to them in the HVO. Therefore, in the work I did, all members including those who spent a month, two, or five in the HVO, regardless of ethnicity, were entitled to receive certain benefits as prescribed on condition that they have the necessary documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, can you look at P 03019. And I believe this might be in the first binder, the bigger binder. This is the order dated June 30th, 1993. It's signed by General --

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. I found a document P 03049, is that the one we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. 3019. There you go. This is a June 30th, 1993 order by General Pekovic in which he is talking about reenforcing units and about different brigades, but when you get to number 8 it says: "All Muslim soldiers who are still active in some units should be disarmed and isolated." So, Mr. Buljan, my question for you regards welfare benefits. If a number of these Muslim soldiers were disarmed and isolated in an all effects were taken out of the HVO, could these same soldiers still later apply for HVO welfare benefits?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If any of these soldiers were disarmed or isolated and left out of the unit, if he had been a member of that unit and if he had -- was wounded or killed, up until then he could apply for a certificate showing how long he had been a member of that unit, and on the basis of that certificate, he could receive all the necessary benefits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yesterday you showed us a document, it was a combination of the reports you had put together. I believe it was the end of 1995 in which you looked at several defence administration, one being Mostar -- or at least one being Mostar, and in that, you counted up the number of killed and wounded and missing. Do agree with me you had access to the soldiers in Mostar who claimed welfare benefits?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I did not. That was a period when we were comparing lists, preparing documents, and whatever we had at the time was presented. From then on, from the beginning of 1992 to the present day, every member of a unit may apply for a certificate about the time spent, what position he held, where he was wounded, how, and so on; so that even today someone who has not realised his rights, he can get medical documents and appear before a commission which will confirm that. I said yesterday that the process hasn't been completed. There are still people who were somewhere else, maybe they spent ten years in a European country after wounding, and then they returned, and when they returned they started to claim their rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. West, I hope I will not interfere with your plan, but there are two questions that I think would be interesting to have an answer to. Mr. Buljan, first some while ago you have spoken about Muslims of some of whom we saw a list, who left after May 9th. And you said they continued to be entitled to benefits if they had the necessary papers. Now, my first question is, was this also limited to damages - to take it globally - that occurred while they still were members of the HVO before leaving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The efforts being made to establish the damage suffered during their stay in the HVO, but again under certain conditions during preparations for the frontline, the time spent on the front line, and returning from the frontline. So if any bodily injury was suffered during that period, it is possible to get medical documents to prove this before a commission and eventually someone can get the status of a war disabled or not if he doesn't have any such bodily injury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You already started answering my second question which would have been, what were the necessary documents? And I take it from you that, of course, it must be proof of identity; and second, there must be some medical documents establishing the causality between the military service and the HVO and the damage that was done. Were there any other documents that the Muslim, in this case, would have to present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what was first and foremost was to -- for the victim to have a certificate which would explicitly say that this person with his first and last name, father's name, his ID number, where he was born, what unit he belonged to, which battalion or company or platoon, and how he suffered damage, was it during execution of the command of the commander or in some other way. This is the first document. If wounding occurred, that same member would have to go and see a doctor, because of the injury, of course, and with the medical documents and this certificate on membership and the circumstances under which he was injured, the commission would establish what the welfare benefit would be depending on the degree of disability. The minimum was 20 percent which would go up to 100 percent. Then there was the first group with 100 percent disability and the second group. Those were the essential document that needed to be collected in the first stage. Later on, some other documents were needed, an ID card, a birth certificate, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I was thinking of a document which you have not now mentioned, so I suppose, but I want to make sure that was not required and that would have been something like a certificate of an honourable discharge, of a correct discharge, sort of a bye-bye letter to put it very in a familiar family way, term.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I must admit that I never asked for such a document. Someone could have spent 15 days in one of the units and may have been very seriously wounded. He may have left that unit and then come back five years later and we would solve his problem. So no discharge letter was requested, but simply a certificate showing his membership and the circumstances under which he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I much appreciate the way in which you have answered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Buljan, just a follow-up on Judge Trechsel's question, if there's an HVO soldier who is, for lack of a better term, kicked out of the HVO, if they are evicted from the HVO, if they are fired from the HVO, can that HVO soldier still receive welfare benefits?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If an HVO member -- you are talking about an HVO member, if he is fired, then that is in another area of consideration. One may be fired because of problems in the unit because of theft, various disciplinary measures. But if we are talking about a healthy combatant, I'm unable to give you an explicit answer. But if it's a victim, people who were injured or wounded were never dismissed from a unit. There was a maximum degree of tolerance, and regardless of when they left, the time spent would always be recognised though there were commissions set up to establish ability, but there was no coercion used to force people to return to the unit if they had lower level wounds, for instance, a wound that healed within 30 days or two months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, keeping in mind the May 9th document that I showed you a few minutes ago, and this June 30th document that you have in front of you now, would you agree that those two documents at least illustrate that the number of HVO Muslim soldiers, at least in Mostar, appears during the course of -- summer of 1993 to be getting smaller and smaller?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I don't know what you are going to say but I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In spite of your instructions, it is my feeling that I'm obliged to make an objection. The witness said that he doesn't know anything about that event, and secondly which is important which has prompted me to stand, the witness is asked to make conclusions on the basis of certain documents. A witness, by definition, is not in the courtroom to make conclusions. He is a fact witness. I believe it is my duty to say this. I'm an officer of the court and regardless of your instructions if such an infringement has been made, I will object.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam West.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, sir, my question regarded the with two documents you had seen. One was dated May 9th, the other was June 30th. And would you agree with me, this comes from your experience as being the head of welfare in the Posavina, but then head of welfare for the republic that these types of orders ultimately led to less numbers of HVO Muslim soldiers in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, if I understand you correctly, Madam, persons who had suffered, applied for their rights, if not within that month, then in a year, five years' time, ten years' time and even today, so there's no dispute. If they prove that they were members of one of the units which no longer exist, and if they have the necessary documents, that can be done even now. So in Posavina, there was no shortage of requests for welfare benefits regardless of ethnicities. They kept making such claims for awhile, he was a member of that unit, afterwards he could have changed the unit or changed whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you just said that in Posavina there was no shortage of request for welfare benefits regardless of ethnicities. Can you tell us whether that same theory applied in Mostar? Were benefits given regardless of ethnicities in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the head of the welfare department, I was concerned with having the proper certificate about the circumstances of the injury and we are talking about the period from the beginning of 1993, 1994, and 1995. I'm talking about Posavina, but this applied later on as well. The essential document was membership in the unit and the circumstances under which the injury was suffered. Such a certificate was signed by the brigade commander. Me as the head of the section and later head of the department could only intervene with respect to the appearance of that certificate requiring perhaps more detailed data or the form it would take. That is what I could do, but I could not force any commander to sign such a certificate or not sign it to change it, amend it, or not, or to make any such request to the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, my question regards Mostar and not Posavina. You said that in Posavina when you were the head, which is 1993, that welfare was distributed without regard to ethnicities. My question, and you can tell me if you do not have the capacity to answer this, is in 1993 was welfare distributed to HVO soldiers regardless of ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, benefits were proved for all wounded members of the HVO, for families of those who had been killed and for the families of war invalids. It was regardless of their ethnicity, but the condition was that they should have some of the basic documents, certificate showing the circumstances under which these individuals were wounded or killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your response you said for all wounded members of the HVO. Is it your testimony that these benefits were distributed in Mostar in 1993 without regard to ethnicity? Do you have the capacity to say yes or no to that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Thank you. I'm not quite sure whether this answer can really be -- this question can really be answered by yes or no. Witness, I'm not sure whether I understood you correctly, but one of your last answers made me think this: You, your office looked at whether the papers were there, if the papers were there, you granted relief, payments, whatever. If there was no paper, there was no way someone could get something from your office, which is an absolutely normal administrative procedure. However, I thought to have understood you as saying that you had no influence on whether the paper was signed because this was done by the commanders, by the military. So you can't perhaps not take a stand and make any comment on in which way the commanders acted, whether commanders the discriminated or not. The way I understand what you have told us so far was beyond your control so you could not know about it. Please tell me if I understood you correctly, and correct me if I understood you wrongly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you've understood me correctly. In 1992, for example, in order to obtain certain benefits, to claim certain rights it would be necessary to have the relevant documents. All those documents were issued by someone. I couldn't issue a birth certificate. I couldn't issue a certificate of marriage. I couldn't issue a certificate on circumstances under which someone was wounded. So if a person came with the relevant document, the documents would be examined and the procedure would be engaged and we would solve the problem then. Whenever there were no documents, we tried to gather the relevant document, supplement them if necessary, and once this was done, then benefits would be granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, Exhibits --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Exhibits 2900604 through 624 are the documents that you brought with you regarding the Posavina. So they were document that you looked at yesterday, and you made the request for them. Do you remember those documents?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that when you had certain information according to which you would be testifying before this Court, you asked the administration for those who were casualties in the homeland war office for these types of documents from the Posavina. Is it your testimony that you personally made the request?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I personally made that request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm not going to go back to those documents. I've reviewed them, and I'm going to give you a summary and tell me if this is about correct. You requested documents for both deceased HVO Muslim members, and you also requested documents for Muslim HVO members who became invalids. And for the 101st HVO Brigade for deceased, I think I counted about 102 Muslims; 106th Brigade, I counted 37; for Bihac, there was 5; Brcko, there was 8; Derventa, there were 91; Odzak, there were 50; Tuzla was 46; Gradacac was 249; and Bosanski Samac was 24. Separately in regard to the invalids: Derventa was 132; Gradacac was 33; Modrica was 48; Odzak was 80; and Tuzla was 9. Is that consistent with your memory reviewing these documents, those numbers; are they about right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one should add that the 102nd Odzak Brigade was included. There should also be the 104th Samac Brigade, 105th Modrica Brigade, there should also be the 106th Orasje Brigade, and 107th Gradacac Brigade. And if you had the 108th in mind when you mentioned Tuzla then that's correct, if not then the 108th HVO Brigade should also be included.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Buljan, would you agree with me that it's those numbers upon which you base your testimony that the HVO treated all of its soldiers well, or equally regardless of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I made that claim well because I could only get that information from Orasje. I said that on the basis of my personal knowledge. Yesterday I said I was the chief of the administration for welfare from mid-1995 until 1998; and then for about two years, I was the deputy director in the federal administration for soldiers from the area, that was at the level of the Federation. So at that time for all HVO members who had the relevant documents, welfare was provided in an identical manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question is, it's these document, these documents that you requested for a certain reason -- strike that. Why did you request these documents then?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is about an entire institution that provided welfare for members of those units. I said that I was appointed in 1992 for the chief of the department. All those who were worked there worked with me and in a certain way I brought the document with me. They remained there, I left. I could only get the documents from them. The documents are still, in a certain sense, kept there, and they are not provided easily. When I was the chief of the department or the administration, there were more people who requested such documents --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question was why did you request these documents? What was in your head when you decided to make a request for these documents? What did you hope that they would show?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these documents show how and in what way one acted, and it shows how many casualties there were in that part of Posavina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I would like my colleague's question to be correctly transcribed. The question concerned the number of Muslims with regard to these documents as I showed these documents. I don't think we are dealing with the number of Muslims who were casualties, we are dealing with Croats and members of other nationalities as well. These documents have been erroneously interpreted by my colleague. So I just wanted to clarify this. These documents weren't asked for only with regard to Muslims but it concerned all those who were casualties regardless of their ethnicity, and that is what the documents are about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, that's correct. The documents do include Muslims, Croats, and other nationalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, I'm going to have to ask you this question again because I think I've misunderstood your answer. When you requested these documents showing casualties of all the HVO soldiers, and you brought them here and you made this request, you testified once you knew that you would be testifying here, what did you hope that they would show the Trial Chamber? How did you expect that he would be interpreted?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above all, my purpose was to show how many casualty there were, to show how they had been wounded. I wanted the documents to show how long this lasted for, that the classifications were made in the way they were made, it could have been done differently. Quite simply, tried to gather certain information in one document in case one wanted explanations. I worked in the office for a long time, and I can provide useful answers with regard to that aspect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since you've come here and testified that -- or part of your testimony is that welfare benefits were given out without regard to ethnicities, and particularly here are issues without regard to whether somebody was Muslim or not, did you understand that this case involved several municipalities that were not included in the Posavina?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that what might be more relevant to our focus here, our records for Muslim HVO soldiers who are from, say, Mostar or areas that are in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't obtain such information when I came here. I said that in a certain sense there were still confidential, not secret; but they are simply not made available. I didn't make them available when I had access to them. There were many who wanted to write books and to consult those documents. I understand why these documents weren't provided, but perhaps if someone else was in Orasje instead of the people I worked with, if that had been the case, I don't think I would have even been given what I was given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question regards whether those documents would be more relevant, would you agree with me that they would be more relevant to us, not whether you could obtain them or not. Do you agree that documents for Mostar would be more relevant to this case?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it would have been better for your case if you had received documents that concern Mostar. They would have been such as they are, and I simply cannot say whether it would have been better for you to have such documents here. But the situation wasn't clear in any military district. In all military districts, I think there were casualties of various ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I understand that you did not make the request for the documents for the areas that are the subject of the indictment. Is it your testimony that you could not have made that request?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I spoke to some people who work in those departments but I understand that they didn't want to me give me that information because others didn't provide that information apart from the information that I managed to obtain, so to speak, on a private basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, after seeing your request to the administration for issues of HVO soldiers and victims in the Croatian war of independence, we made the same request about one month ago. Can you look at P 10810. 10810. Mr. Buljan, I believe it's in the binder at your feet. Sorry. You have that there?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 10810; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you. You should go after the tab, it's 10810 -- Mr. Buljan, I think you are on the wrong page. If you go after the tab.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, maybe we could have some assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There you go. And the B/C/S is behind the English. Mr. Buljan, I would just like to flip through these documents with you, and this was a request that we made once we saw your request. We made the same request, but we made it for the municipalities that are listed in the indictment. I think that's a total of 28 municipalities and as of yesterday we had responses from 11. So if you go to the B/C/S which there's a Bates stamp that ends in 145. This is page 1 of the English. It's a record from the Jablanica, do you see that? You have it right there.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a record --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would kindly ask [Overlapping speakers] to provide us with information whether that was disclosed to us. I made the fast checking via e-court, and I was not able to find it. Perhaps it was too short check, but maybe we should be given this information because I suspect, I'm almost sure, I'm not entirely sure, but I'm almost sure that we did not got this as disclosure from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We received this night before last. I think it's in the binders, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is no doubt it is in binders, so we got it yesterday, and we have it today. But that doesn't -- it is not in accordance with the rule. This should have been disclosed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, we made a request of these documents as a results of looking at their exhibits. There's no requirement that we would have disclose these earlier. It's -- it would be quite unusual to believe that we could have ever anticipated requesting these documents in order to have disclosed them earlier. Again, they were requested as a result of looking at the Defence exhibits. There's no way we could have disclosed these earlier. Furthermore, this is on cross-examination. They are not require to be on the 65 ter list. They go directly to the issue of credibility of the witness and also in direct opposition to the Defence case upon which this witness is purporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in front of you, you have what is Bates staffed at the bottom 145, this is a record from Jablanica and it says: "In reference to your request attached find the registry file for Avdo Velic." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you said it was my request. I didn't speak to this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Buljan, I think there must be a misunderstanding. This is not your request. This is our request. I just want to review these documents with you slowly, if you can bear with that, then we'll talk about them. So that is the first one from Jablanica. If you can go to page 4 of the English, but it's 2147 of the B/C/S, it's Bates stamped 2147 at the bottom. This is a record from Vares in response to our request, they gave us the record of Edin Brkovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have to answer verbally out loud. Now, if you can to page 9 of the English which is Bates stamped 21540 of the B/C/S. That is record from Stolac, and they responded from a one record of a Huso Obradovic. Do you see that? I believe the witness is not getting translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The witness is not getting translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you hear what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you go to the B/C/S stamped 2150, it's a record from Stolac. When I say stamped 2150, you'll see a stamp of numbers on these records. Every page has a number, and the 2150 is the last four digits. There you go. So that's record from Stolac and they responded with a record of one person which is Huso Obradovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you can go to page 2155 of the B/C/S which is page 18 of the English?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness is kindly asked to speak a little more loudly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a record from Konjic and here they give us three names: Edin Hrhotbegovic [phoen], Senahid Donjo [phoen], and Tomislav Markovic [phoen]. Do you see those three names?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you go to 2159 of the B/C/S, page 23 of the English. These are records from Busovaca, in which they give us two names, the first is Elvir Cecic [phoen], the second is Alic Admir. Do you see those?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go to the B/C/S 2163. This is the Fojnica records. 2163, they indicate that they have no members of the Bosniak ethnicity who were responsive to our request. Do you see that? You have to say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go to 2164. This is Kresevo. And they also indicate that they have no records, and no one has ever received compensation on those grounds, no response to our request, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. I apologise to my colleague. Could we perhaps be a little more precise. In these documents, I see that we are only dealing with soldiers who were killed, not a single member of the HVO was killed of a Bosniak nationality was recorded. We have two categories, so this is the page that my colleague referred to it has to do with Kresevo municipality because the answers of the various municipalities are different. Some concern war invalids, and some concern those who were killed. So if we are going through this very quickly, well, we should see what the answer is, in fact. Does it only concern those who are wounded or does it only concern those who are killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, don't waste your time and the Chamber's time which is precious. You asked for information on Muslim soldiers from the HVO who were killed. The authorities on the 10th of February of this year sent you their replies. I've been through these documents very rapidly, and I see that the HVO soldiers who were killed in 1992, 1993, all this is spread over time. At least two of them I see were killed outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina and so one may ask oneself what they were doing there. So we are not going to examine all the details for all these examples, but put your questions to the witness to demonstrate what you, in fact, want to demonstrate.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to be absolutely clear, in the first instance, I may have misspoke. But these are not records of HVO Muslim soldiers who were killed. The records of HVO Muslim soldiers who were killed, and their families received benefits from the HVO. So this is not a combination of those who were killed. There are 11 municipalities as I said in the very beginning, and I was going over those particular 11, but I can do this much more quickly. With the Trial Chamber's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm just going to review these records and purport to you what I believe they say, which is in Jablanica there was one Muslim HVO soldier who was killed and whose family received benefits from the HVO. In Vares there was one; in Stolac there was one; in Konjic there were 3; in Busovaca there was 2; Punica [phoen] was zero; Kresevo was zero; Travnik was zero; Grude was zero; Kakanjac was one; and in Citluk was zero. Now, my question to you, Mr. Buljan, is would you agree with me that these records paint a very different picture of the dispersement of welfare benefits to the diseased Muslim soldiers than the records that you brought from Posavina?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I don't see any approval for benefits. These are just the number of those who were killed. There is no indication that Avdo or whatever his name is received so much. There was just an answer to your question that he was a member and that he was taken care of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you'll agree with me that these are members who were ultimately taken care of by the welfare department?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would also agree that these numbers that we have looked at are significantly smaller than the numbers that you presented this Court in the Posavina records?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt these numbers, but I must say that the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina did not begin at the same time, the same hour in all municipalities. Some waged war earlier, some later on, some for longer periods of time and others for shorter periods of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you go to P 02945. I believe that's in the first binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Excuse me, my mistake, that is not in the binder. It is a document that you were shown yesterday. And if we could have that in e-court. It's P 02945. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing this document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking at it now. It is a command on appointments in the Rama Brigade command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. And you were shown it yesterday because you pointed out that number 20 - and you don't have to look at it now - was the social welfare clerk that was appointed by Bruno Stojic in this particular command. Do you remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to that one appointment, there's a total of 80 appointments in this document, and they are ranging from SIS officers, to IPD officers, to artillery officer, intelligence officer, battalion commanders. Mr. Buljan, is it fair to say that all these appointments were made at the same time by Bruno Stojic, at the same time as the social welfare clerk and they took effect at the same time?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't confirm that, that this happened at the same time and the clerk for welfare was not appointed by Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday when you spoke of number 20, that is listed on page 8 of the English in this document, who was he appointed by?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person was appointed, so this is in the brigade command. If we are talking about this document, you said you were talking about the welfare administration. Bruno Stojic did not appoint people to that welfare administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Buljan, all the things that you provided to the disabled soldiers and the family of the deceased soldiers, whether it be rehabilitation, hospitalisation, accommodation or just money, do those things, it required that your department have money; correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you had some type of budget; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have a budget. We had estimates made per month, and we made requests for that sum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the source of funding for the welfare provisions and the money for the families?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first funds which were allotted, I'll go back briefly to Posavina as the head of the administration there were granted when Derventa fell on the 4th of July, 1992. This was a small sum of money, and my colleague commander and myself requested from Derventa municipality to find ways, whatever ways to find the funds for us to distribute to members of the army and the families of the killed. Derventa fell, the army units were being reduced in numbers, and we wanted to provide funds. The second time was when Bosanski Brod fell and the whole municipality of Derventa on the 6th of October, 1992. I was in the command in or Oreovac [phoen], it's a place in Croatia close to Slavonski Brod, and the army was housed throughout that area in abandoned schools and houses. I was visited by the representative of the Bosnia-Herzegovina embassy, there were five or six people, and I, among others, spoke to them and they offered assistance. That group which came to visit us included my professor, Avdo Halilovic, who taught Serbo-Croatia when I went to secondary school in Derventa; and I told them that we needed certain funds to distribute them to the men and that we intended to go back to the theatre of war in Posavina so as to keep the soldiers there. He answered that he would see what he could do and that he would let us know. The next day he came and brought with him 90.000 German marks. We took over that sum. The head of finance found somewhere else, I don't know how, whether this may have been earlier savings in the municipality from companies, I don't know, and we distributed those funds. Those were the first remunerations. Later on, the funds were provided through the brigades, they were not on a regular basis. They were not large, and the first funds collected through the department for welfare, which I signed was in August 1994. And this was a letter that I addressed to the military district or the head of the administration for welfare, I can't be quite sure about that, whether it was towards the finance department or military district or the finances of the welfare administration which was then based in Citluk, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, did you receive any money from the Defence Department in 1993?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked for funds through the finances of the military district. Now, whether that came from the Defence Department or not, I cannot answer with certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you go to 2D 01245.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. West, the last answer, Mr. Buljan, perhaps this is a matter of translation. You were asked whether you obtained money from Defence Department, and your answer says that you requested money. But it does not said that you also received it. Could you complete the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, towards the end of 1993, that is the last quarter of 1993, funds did come through the brigade commander who would make a request. I must be sincere, I don't know where they came from, whether they came from the Defence Department or somewhere else. Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, 2D 01245. It's in the second binder, excuse me. 1245. This is an exhibit you actually looked at yesterday with Ms. Nozica. And it's a letter to the Ministry of Defence in Croatia and it regards remunerations for a soldier who was a Muslim soldier. Do you remember looking at this?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the top of this letter says that it indicates that it's responding to a letter from Croatia. It says: "With regard to your letter," gives a number "of 14 July." Do you agree with me that this is a response to something that Croatia was asking?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, clearly it's a response to a request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why Croatia was asking about this?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must tell you that it wasn't Croatia but the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and I must say in those days there wasn't a single institution that didn't have a special feeling towards wounded soldiers and families of the killed. So I wouldn't be surprised if there were other documents when any other institution may be informing an official institution about certain funds. I would often be addressed to with inquiries similar to these, so clearly somebody had addressed somebody in the Ministry of Defence and then that is how this letter came about asking the commander whether those funds were paid out or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, what do you mean by special feeling, that the Ministry of Defence had a special feeling about this?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean is that all institutions in all states had a kind of specific view and opinion and wanted to assist soldiers. If this person had addressed the Ministry of Forestry in the Republic of Croatia, I wouldn't be surprised if a similar answer were to be received, to religious institutions, the media, because simply everyone wanted to assist in such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the case of welfare benefits, would that assistance include paying for those benefits?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a brigade, which had more funds, which was on its own territory, which was able to obtain funds from certain sources, then it may have made better remunerations in relation to other brigade. This went on until funds started to be distributed through the welfare department when everything was consolidated in one spot, and then every rank received the same benefit for the same disability. So until this welfare was organised properly, the distribution of funds varied. So I can't tell you whether somebody in the 103rd Brigade got less, than somebody in a 104th more. But when this started to work in an organised fashion, it was all equal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, do you agree with me that the Ministry of Defence for the Republic of Croatia paid for the welfare benefits for the HVO soldiers of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they paid for the welfare of soldiers, members of the HVO in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I personally, through the welfare organisation in the Republic of Croatia, would sometime request a place to be found for rehabilitation or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to P 10772. Binder number 1, the bigger binder. 10772. And the front is the English, but I believe the last -- you just had it, there you go. The last page is the B/C/S. And this is an interview with Ivica Rajic, who was the prime minister of Croatia. I'm going to go to the bottom of the English and the -- bottom first page in the top, second page, and he speaks about coming into office, and he says: "We've stopped transferring soldiers directly between the Croatian Armed Forces and the Croat Defence council, the Bosnian Croat component of the Bosnian Federation's armed forces. We have also severe direct communications and control links between the two militaries. Moreover, since signing a financial assistance agreement with the Bosnian Federation in May, financial transfers between Croatia and the Federation Defence ministry have become transparent. Croatia is not, however, abandoning the Bosnian Croats. It is simply looking to find durable long term solutions that balance their legitimate interests with those of viable Bosnian state and of the countries Serb and Bosniak communities. Croatia will continue --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. "Croatia will continue to pay military pensions and disability allowances to Bosnian Croats, but these payment will in future either be made via the appropriate federal institutions or paid directly to beneficiaries in as open a manner as possible. They will no longer be channelled through shady, parallel structures."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that your response to my question about whether you knew Croatia was paying for the welfare benefits for the HVO soldier was I don't know, but subsequent to that period of time did you become aware that this issue was in the newspapers?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that. That it was discussed in the newspapers. I must say that I, as head of the welfare department, never sought any funds for the salaries of the members and wounded members of the homeland war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, did HVO benefits include giving welfare benefits for those soldiers who were not permanent members of the -- can you hear me? Mr. Buljan, can you hear me? My question is --

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can. But I've lost the interpretation for a moment. So could the last two sentences be reinterpreted for me, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Did the HVO also pay welfare benefits for those soldiers who were not permanent members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really have to intervene. My client and the others, other accused are reacting, but this is a hypothetical question that it is impossible to answer to whom, when, in what period, which HVO, who was paying it? I think it's an imprecise question, so it should be made more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam West, will you specify your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... interrupt anyway. This question implies that there was the answer or that there is evidence that there was something called permanent members or sorry not permanent members. We don't know so far, nothing about that category. So, of course, first, that should be established, then the second question should be asked. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam West, please try and make it more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must remind you that you have another 23 or so minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, were there any soldiers fighting in the HVO in Posavina when you were involved that were members of other armed forces, for example, the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were members and volunteers from the Croatian army in Bosanska Posavina. They were mostly people who were born in Bosanska Posavina or the environs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the HVO paid for their possible welfare benefits if they were injured or wounded or killed, did that money come from Croatia as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment. I don't like to intervene but regarding the translation I have a little problem. Madam West is asking you a question, were there soldiers in the Posavina HVO who were members of other armed forces, for example, the Croatian army. So the question is very precise. I'd like you to answer slowly so there should be no mistakes in the translation . Please answer Madam West's question but answer it with precision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will do my best and repeat my answer. There were members of the Croatian army who came to the territory of Bosanska Posavina and who fought in Bosanska Posavina. They were mostly born in Bosanska Posavina and before the war broke out, they were somewhere in Croatia in one of the Croatian units.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me take advantage of the pause, you have noticed correctly on page 32, line 21 and 24 there is the answer that the witness said, "Yes, there were members and volunteers." The witness didn't say that. Everyone listening, he didn't say "and volunteers", he said "volunteers". That's probably why you reacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is why I put the question to him once again. You are quite right, Madam Nozica. In line 22 he said, "There were members and volunteers." I have made him answer again more clearly and in his answer we don't see the word volunteers anymore. So you see, sir, it's very important, perhaps you don't realise it, but for counsel and for the Judges, it is important. I wish to specify the question further. These soldiers who belonged to the Croatian army, who were born in Posavina, did they come to the HVO of Posavina as volunteers and were integrated in the HVO, or as one might conclude from line 22, there were members of the Croatian army and volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct that members of the Croatian army who were mostly born in Bosanska Posavina came to assist in the war in Posavina. When their village was occupied, they felt that they could be of assistance and they came. Some of them would stay with us for good, others would go back. And others would leave the army altogether, some were wounded, some were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You haven't understood my question. What I wanted to know is did they come as volunteers or not? That is the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They came as volunteers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So they came as volunteers. Madam west, continue, please. I said five to, so that we should only have one break, so please continue and then we'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, when these Croatian army volunteers came to fight in the Posavina, is it your testimony that some of them stayed and then some of them returned to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And when they came to fight for the HVO, who paid their salaries?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were in the HVO, they were paid by the HVO when they had the funds. The volunteers who were not members of the HVO, I don't know who paid them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you go to P 00153. 00153. I think you have it right there, it's behind it. Thank you. You have the B/C/S in front of you. And this is a letter, it's a Republic of Croatia, Ministry of Defence letter and it says: "The request of the chief inspector of the Defence General Martin Spegelj for sending a part of the soldiers and officers of the operation zone Rijeka mainly Croats and Muslims ready to voluntarily go to BaiHto help struggle of the people of the BiH has been accepted by the top-ranking military authorities." Says: "The general headquarters of the Croatian army concurs and supports this idea, with the suggestion that this group for a start, number 300 to 400 soldiers and officers." It then says: "They are to be sent under the command of Major Mustafa and other officers with different military equipment, weaponry and ammunition. All who go, retain all the rights of HV soldiers, including monthly salaries. They cannot wear HV insignia on their uniforms, nor can they hold other documents used by members of the HV. The task is an urgent one, and the execution of it is to be commenced immediately. Should the situation develop favourably, sending of other groups, i.e., reinforcements of this one, is not to be excluded." Mr. Buljan, in your capacity as the head of welfare, you had indicated yesterday that the soldiers to which you gave welfare benefits also received salaries from their own units, and I'm talking about the HVO units. Would you agree with me that the volunteers who came from the Republic of Croatia were actually paid by the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STIPO BULJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document signed by General Petar Stipetic supports such an interpretation. As to whether that was actually the case, I can't say. I don't know whether this was actually put into practice. This is now the 1992, many things haven't been resolved at the time, so quite frequently the documents drafted were not documents that would be fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Buljan, thank you for your very candid answers. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. West. We will now have the break that Mr. Karnavas so desires, and we will resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon Your Honours. As you can see, the absence of my client, Dr. Prlic, his absence is as a result of having spent some time with him during the break, going over an unofficial translation of your decision concerning his supplemental to his statement. The concerns obviously are the reasoning, the reasoning that the Trial Chamber has presented. One, claiming that it looks too much like a expert report. Well, one must forgive Dr. Prlic for being an intelligent human being and fro having the education and the wherewithal to spend two years putting together that report, in his way, in his fashion, of course, keeping in mind that he has authored about a half a dozen to a dozen books. Two, the Court's reasoning that we cross-examined Tomljanovich, and this has been a sore point for us many, many months now. If you look at the Popovic case they cross-examine witnesses for days and days. We get hours, sometimes minutes. To say that we had adequate time to cross-examine Tomljanovich is simply illogical, in my point, and I'm trying to be as measured as I possibly can thinking back to the complexity of the Tomljanovich report and the amount of time that was provided. Frankly, it was shocking. The third reasoning, you state is that Dr. Prlic could have testified. Well, as we indicated, you don't give us enough time to put on our witnesses and so what you want now is to say, Well, present less evidence in your Defence and then take the stand, this way you don't have to put together a 600-page report attacking William Tomljanovich, the Prosecution employee, employee, who is called an analyst/expert. So frankly for all of these reasons, Dr. Prlic feels that at this point it is quite evident that the Trial Chamber is being rather inflexible. The Trial Chamber could have very easily accepted the report and then said, Well, not going to give any weight to it. But the reasoning is rather -- is such that gives him great pause as to whether he is getting a fair trial, whether the result will ever be fair, and whether he will ever even have an opportunity to see liberty as a free man again. So for those reasons, he does not wish to participate for the remainder of the proceedings. He did give me instructions that he wishes for me to move for certification, and he would like me to do so at this particular moment, keeping in mind that the Prosecution of course has the opportunity to respond, but I am making an oral motion for certification to appeal this decision, and of course pending the Court's decision on that, Dr. Prlic will then consider what his other options are. It is rather regrettable that Dr. Prlic who has not missed a single second, who has not been disruptive, who has asked only a few questions, very measured ones, who has made a couple of statements, again very measured ones, should find himself in this position to the point where he does not wish to participate any further in the proceedings because it is his perception, and one that I share, that based on this decision it appears that the Trial Chamber is extremely inflexible as much as it claims to be very flexible, as much as it claim that is it wishes to be fair, that from this decision it seems that any amount of flexibility is merely words to be uttered but no deeds to be seen from that. And so as a result of that, Dr. Prlic, as I've indicated, does not wish to come out to participate any further. In keeping with what we saw from another accused and that was Mr. Coric who obviously walked out especially after the Trial Chamber in showing its flexibility to the Prosecution said they could begin their cross-examination the following day when 45 minutes was left on the clock, the Prosecution had months to prepare the cross-examination, had spent three days plus more getting a statement from that particular witness, and came up with a farcical, a farcical excuse as to why cross-examination could not start on that. That's why Mr. Coric left. That's why Dr. Prlic was upset as well, and I'm sure others were; and now this decision coming on top of that demonstrates to Dr. Prlic that perhaps the things that are to come have already been predetermined. I'm not saying that that is the case, but that is the perception that is that is growing ever so more every day that this case proceeds. And so I regret that I have to make these submissions, but these are the submissions based on the instructions that I've been give. And as I've indicated, please consider this an oral motion for certification of your decision to deny his supplement to his opening statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecution, I don't know if you want to respond orally right now or whether you would prefer to file written submissions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That was going to be my request, Mr. President. It's -- without going to the substance of the ruling, I think that it's likely that the Trial Chamber and ultimately the Appeals Chamber would benefit if this were -- if, in fact, an appeal is certified. And I don't know what the Prosecution position is going to be on that point. But I'd suggest that the normal course, which is a written application in which the Defence lays out its argument, why certification in its view should be granted, would be appropriate. It would then enable the Prosecution to file a written response, which possibly both of which the two parties positions on this would be of benefit to the Trial Chamber in the ruling that it ultimately issues. And so our preference or our suggestion would be understanding that Mr. Karnavas and his client are feeling strongly at the moment, that we proceed with written submissions on the application for certification to which the Prosecution then would file its written response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I frankly would wonder whether it would not be also preferable that Mr. Karnavas put his request in writing. After all the proceeding is relatively formal, and there are very specific reasons to be raised. You have said a lot of things, Mr. Karnavas, but it is not really in the form of such a request for certification. I'm sure it can be done tomorrow morning, knowing your proficiency, and I would feel safer than taking a decision on the basis of your oral submissions today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We will do that, Mr. President, Your Honours. I was acting on instructions to make that oral request, and also to pass along my client's sentiments which I've done so. Perhaps more vigorously than might have been expected of my client, but, nonetheless, the record has been made, and yes we will be filing something in writing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Kovacic, I think there's something that you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Your Honours, for allocating a minute to me. Today at the beginning of the hearing, to be more precise at 1430 hours, we filed a request for an IC number. We objected to the suggestion made yesterday by the Prosecution -- not yesterday's suggestion, but the suggestion for tendering a document into evidence in relation to Mr. Bozic on the basis of your decision on the guide-lines dated the 24th of April, chapter 8, guide-lines 8, in fact, paragraph 32, item 1D, it say that is we should have done this at the beginning of each hearing. As you can see from what I have said, we were 15 minutes or rather 17 minutes late because the hearing begins at 1415 hours. The beginning, I think one understands the beginning in a flexible way. For technical reasons, we weren't able to send the mail before half past 2, although everything was ready in the morning, so I would be grateful if you could admit this into evidence and if an IC number could be provided so when you do decide on this suggestion please bear this in mind. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll confer with my judges immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the microphone is on and while you were conferring, perhaps I can just point out as well we did also, on behalf of Mr. Stojic, file a motion, I think, just before Your Honours came in objecting to the Prosecution bid to tender as an exhibit the interview that they conducted with the last witness, so I would join the application that Your Honours do receive that application and consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If, in fact, the Chamber said that it was necessary to file the document before -- just before the hearing, well, under certain circumstances if it's a little late, half an hour late, we won't dismiss such a request because it's a few minutes late. So the Chamber agrees to this suggestion and as usual we will demonstrate our flexibility. Could the Registrar please provide us with a number. Just a minute we'll first have a number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Praljak Defence's opposition to the Prosecution's exhibits entered through witness Slobodan Bozic shall be given number IC 920. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, is that why you are on your feet? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's something called Sense that functions within the Tribunal. It's some sort of official organisation that informs the public in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in writing and through images and the public is informed about the events before the Court, before the Tribunal. I'd like to read out an article, a recent article that concerns the following: I quote: "Two days later after the 21st, so on the 23rd, the then commander of the HVO Main Staff Slobodan Praljak issued an order that is as follows: Sort out the situation in Vares and don't do any mercy to anyone. When carrying out the order, the HVO units under the command of Ivica Rajic killed 31 civilians of Muslim nationality in Stupni Dol." So when carrying out my order, that's what it says here, under the command of Rajic, it's from the Sense organisation, this is what the public in Bosnia and Herzegovina can read. As the official version of what was discussed here, I'm not going to go into how this was presented here about the time-frames we referred to and so on and so forth, but this is biased. It publicly provides incorrect information, and it's an act of media lynching and this is being systematically done by Sense. This has been the case for years. This can't continue, you've seen those documents here. You've seen the dates. You've seen the time when everything was forwarded. And you will take a decision at the end that is going to be your decision, but at least several million people have had access to this information here, guilt has been established, judgements have been handed down, families and entire people has to live in such conditions since we can't speak to journalist. The Judges has forbidden us from doing this. I think the Registry, the Prosecution, and the Judges themselves should ban such things or punish such things otherwise there is no purpose to this case. We could conclude this case tomorrow. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have publicly corrected this information. Your counsel can obviously contact any legal body to correct false information. I don't where this press agency is located but there are legal procedures that make it possible to act because one has violated the presumption of innocence, that principle. It's important that evidence is not erroneously conveyed and the Chamber mustn't draw the wrong conclusions. So we'll see what we can do because our mission is also to ensure that the presumption of innocence is a principle that is respected, that you should see what the procedures are, you should consult your counsel and see what you can do with regard to this press agency that misrepresented the information or document that was referred to in the course of the proceedings. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, but, you see, what I think you could do is that this shouldn't be called the Tribunal. They are hiding behind the word "Tribunal." I wouldn't like to quarrel with the media journalists and their interpretations, but it says here Sense Tribunal. That is you, the Prosecution, the Registry, and international organisation that is endeavouring to establish the truth. This is impermissible, but all the media falsehoods, the lies, the fabrications is something I wouldn't go into. I've lived long enough to know that. I would just suggest that the word Tribunal be redacted because that represents you, and you are included under the word Tribunal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic should address the officer of the court. The article, something we are not familiar with, we don't know anything about it. So if your lawyer is here, he can communicate it to the Chamber, and we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I actually, I have the feeling that it is not really a matter which directly comes under the authority of the Chamber. It's a matter probably to be dealt with the court Registry, maybe the president of the Court, but it is of a greater importance than what this Chamber does and I suggest, although it's not really for me to do much in that sense, but I would suggest that Mr. Kovacic really address the Registry and takes the necessary steps, he probably knows much better than I do, what the steps are. I share your feelings, Mr. Praljak, that this is outrageous, and I'm sure something can and will be done to it. This is not, I think, any lack of goodwill of the Chamber, but it's just a matter of the organisation. And I see you do not insist that it's us personally who act, but I think something must be done and will probably be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, one separate matter going back to page 42, line 14, notice that an IC number was given to my learned friend's motion. The motion filed by us was filed just before 2.15, and I stand to be corrected, perhaps we don't need an IC number because we properly filed it; but I just wanted to alert the Registrar to that fact if we do need an IC number one has not been given so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic, independently of what my colleague has said, I, in my personal name would like to have the mentioned article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And I thank Judge Trechsel. In any event, thank you for your good advice. We will certainly take steps. My client has clearly explained what it is all about, and he believes, and I agree with him, that it would -- that it is a good idea for the Chamber to be informed about it. The agency, Sense, as Mr. Praljak has said is not a component part of the Tribunal, but it is factually in the building of this Tribunal. It has its own office, and the design of their web page is such that any reader who is not familiar with the detailed structure of the Tribunal can objectively consider it to be an organ or an agency of the Tribunal. And in the press, in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, for your information, this is stated that this was such and such a thing was published by an agency attached to the ICTY, the Sense agency. But, of course, if you were to ask them, they would say we are independent, we have nothing to do with that, but we will, of course, consider the possible steps to be taken with respect to Sense.
